newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK shadow legislature meets despite legal threat.
newsitem.headline: HK shadow legislature meets despite legal threat.

text.p: The shadow Hong Kong legislature set up by Beijing met informally in the territory on Friday despite threats it could be sued if it operated on Hong Kong soil before the colony reverts to China on July 1.
Rita Fan, president of the provisional assembly, played down the breakfast gathering of panels dealing with procedural and administrative matters, calling it informal.
"We are definitely not creating two power centres," Fan said outside the meeting's venue across the road from the current legislature.

Ironically, the spot was The Hong Kong Club, the territory's oldest club and regarded by some as a bastion of the British colonial establishment. Until now the provisional legislature has met across the border in the Chinese city of Shenzhen.

Martin Lee, head of the Democratic Party, Hong Kong's largest, has threatened to sue the shadow body if it meets in Hong Kong on the grounds that it is unconstitutional to have two legislatures operating at the same time. Lee was in Europe on Friday but his deputy, Yeung Sum, told Reuters he doubted the party would consider Friday's meeting a formal session of the shadow legislature.

Fan said any panels would not be formally established until February 22 when the provisional chamber would endorse them, and that Friday's meeting had merely been to gather members' views on what sort of issues the panels should deal with.
A small group of pro-democracy activists protested outside the Hong Kong Club, condemning the provisional legislature.
Fan said future meetings would continue to be held in Shenzhen.

"In order to respect the authority governing Hong Kong, I think it is best we do not hold our official meetings of the Provisional Legislative Council in Hong Kong while it is still being ruled as a British colony," Fan said.

The provisional body was chosen by a China-approved caucus last December. It will make Hong Kong's laws after the July 1 handover, and is expected to undo the democratic reforms enacted under Governor Chris Patten in the last days of British rule.
Britain and the pro-democracy movement in Hong Kong say the move is illegal under the 1984 Sino-British treaty that set out the framework of the return of Hong Kong to China.
